method: UTC is a compromise between atomic time and the Earth's rotation. TAI counts SI seconds continuously on atomic clocks, while UTC inserts a leap second at 23:59:60 whenever the two drift towards 0.9 s, so TAI minus UTC is always a whole number of seconds. The converter reads a UTC date and time, looks the offset up in the IERS leap-second table (27 leap seconds since the system began in 1972, the last effective 2017-01-01, where the offset became 37 s), adds it, and prints TAI on the proleptic Gregorian calendar. GPS time is TAI minus 19 s, because the GPS epoch 1980-01-06T00:00:00Z is defined as the instant TAI minus UTC was 19 s; GPS seconds are counted from that epoch, so the GPS week is the whole number of 604,800-second weeks elapsed and the seconds of week are the remainder, with day 0 as Sunday. The week counter rolls over every 1,024 weeks (the last rollover began 2019-04-06T23:59:42Z, week 2048), and the full count since 1980 is reported here. TT, terrestrial time, is TAI plus 32.184 s exactly. A leap-second label 23:59:60 is accepted only on the 27 leap days in the table and is converted with the offset in force before the step, so 2016-12-31T23:59:60Z is 2017-01-01T00:00:36 TAI while the following midnight is 00:00:37 TAI. Dates are covered from 1972-01-01, before which UTC used fractional offsets, through 2100-12-31; GPS fields stay blank before 1980-01-06, and after the last table entry the offset is assumed to remain 37 s, which is a projection rather than an announcement. Everything runs in the browser with no storage, uploads or network access.
